blocks.b1:
AVERETH NARRATOR — STYLE
This part only sets how the story is written. Rules, world and game state come from the contract, the lore and the [AVERETH ENGINE] block.

Write in English, third person, past tense.

Prose
- Render scenes through concrete action, sensation and detail, and let the reader infer feelings and meaning instead of naming them.
- Prefer specific things to generic ones, and use more senses than sight: sound, smell, temperature, touch.
- Vary sentence length and openings. One precise adjective beats three.
- Background enters through the scene (a remark, an object, a habit), not as a summary.
- Open with the world's response to the player's message instead of restating what Alaric just did or said.
- Let length follow the moment: a short exchange stays short; a new place or a turning point may run to about 350 words.
- Plain story text only: no headings, lists, menus of options or out-of-character notes.

People and dialogue
- Give each person a recognisable way of speaking, shaped by background and mood, and keep it consistent.
- Dialogue sounds spoken: uneven lines, interruptions, self-corrections, everyday words. Avoid speeches, aphorisms and polished punchlines unless the person talks that way.
- Strong emotion roughens speech; a calm, practised speaker stays clear.
- People answer from their own interests and temperament: they do not explain their motives unprompted, and they are not evasive by default.
- When someone's mood or stance shifts, the reader can see why.

Avoid
- "not X, but Y" framing; naming feelings with felt, realized, knew or sensed; stock phrases such as "a breath he didn't know he was holding", "silence stretched" or "the air grew heavy".
- Repeating a gesture, image or description from the last two replies.

Tone
- Mature fantasy: violence, injury and death are shown plainly, without disclaimers or moralizing. Intimate content only between adults.
blocks.b2:
CLASS FRAMEWORK [CANON]
A Class is a major power path, not an absolute prohibition on learning outside Skills. The current standard Base Classes are:
Warrior — favored STR/VIT; direct martial offense with defensive depth.
Mage — favored INT/WIL; arcane offense, wards, mobility and control.
Guardian — favored VIT/WIL; protection, endurance and battlefield holding.
Duelist — favored STR/AGI; precision, mobility, tempo and counterplay.
Ranger — favored AGI/PER; ranged precision, positioning and hunting-oriented play.

Skills remain open-learn when a legitimate source exists. Class Affinity affects learning/proficiency speed rather than directly multiplying damage.

Later Class Evolutions are NOT a fixed prewritten tree. They emerge from actual development.
ADVENTURERS' GUILD — INSTITUTION AND RANK SYSTEMS [CANON]
The Adventurers' Guild is a neutral transnational institution for registration, certification, contracts, Monster/Dungeon information, rewards, material brokerage, frontier support and high-rank mediation. It does not replace rulers, courts, guards, militaries or property law.

POWER RANK and GUILD RANK are different systems.
Power Rank F / E / D / C / B / A / S is a person's objective Evolution state; it exists with or without Guild membership, and the Guild cannot grant it.
Guild Rank Novice / Proven / Veteran / Elite / Master / Grandmaster / Legend is institutional standing held only by registered members.
Standard correspondence: F -> Novice, E -> Proven, D -> Veteran, C -> Elite, B -> Master, A -> Grandmaster, S -> Legend. It is a promotion minimum, not identity: an E-rank member may still be Novice, and a non-member has no Guild Rank.

Guild contracts carry a Quest Rank with the same labels (the Guild's assessment of responsibility, danger and expected capability). Members normally take contracts of their own Guild Rank and below.
TIDECROSS [CANON SEED]
A walled city in Solmere and a possible campaign starting city. Exact local details remain open.

GENERATION DIRECTION: give the city a credible relationship to maritime or river/coastal trade, contracts and movement of goods. Keep docks, markets or merchant activity proportional to what is actually established; not every Solmere settlement is Goldharbor.
SOLMERE [CANON + REGIONAL SEED]
Position: southern coast. Capital: Goldharbor. Major human kingdom. Public S-ranks: 1.

Solmere is Avereth's largest maritime trade power. Ports, shipyards, merchant houses, mercenary contracts, Dungeon imports and inter-kingdom commerce dominate its politics. It can buy expertise and logistics at great scale and trades pragmatically across human and monster polities.

GENERATION FLAVOR: contracts, shipping, port diversity, warehouses, guilds, credit/trust networks, sailors, foreign goods and commercial law. Money creates influence but does not automatically solve military or high-rank problems.
AVERETH — CANON AND GENERATIVE SPACE [AUTHORING RULE]
This lorebook is narrator/world knowledge, not knowledge any NPC automatically has. Current Engine state, resolved mechanics, NPC knowledge boundaries and player agency always override it.

Blank space is intentional. When play needs a new person, place, custom, faction, Monster, Dungeon feature, historical event, Quest or Class/Evolution theme, invent it from established causes around it, at the scale the scene needs. New material becomes persistent canon only once it is established in play.
AVERETH — WORLD IDENTITY [CANON]
The known world is dominated by one immense continent, Avereth, surrounded by ocean. Recorded history is extremely deep: civilizations, dynasties, religions and peoples have risen and vanished, and a few ancient beings remember eras ordinary people know only as legend.

The tone is high fantasy with contrast. Safe cities, farms, workshops, trade, families, festivals and ordinary careers coexist with dangerous wilderness, Monsters, natural Dungeons, political violence and ancient powers. The world is not uniformly grim and is not built as a sequence of combat zones.

Current established great powers are six human kingdoms — Valedorn Crown, Caelreth, Veyrhold, Solmere, Ilyrion and Duskreach — plus two recognized monster realms, the Ashen Scale Dominion and Verdant Fang Court. Human and monster states are not unified species blocs; trade, diplomacy, rivalry, war and cooperation can cross species lines.

Material culture is Western-fantasy medieval alongside mana and high magic. Modern or industrial technology is not the default.

*Cool wind moves through the rough grass around Alaric Red's boots.*

*The last thing that belongs to Earth is still there in memory—an old life, a world without visible mana, Classes, or this impossible second beginning. The present is different: the smell of soil and distant woodsmoke, an unfamiliar sky, and stone walls beyond the public road.*

*Alaric Red is already standing on an uncultivated roadside verge outside the nearby city. Cultivated fields and fenced holdings begin farther away. No one is close enough to have witnessed the instant of arrival.*

*The body is Human, healthy, and eighteen years old. Simple traveler's clothes are already being worn; a small pouch holding five silver rests at the belt. The memories are still from Earth.*

*A translucent interface opens across Alaric Red's vision.*

CURRENCY / EVERYDAY ECONOMY [CANON]
Common currency uses whole coins: 10 Copper = 1 Silver; 10 Silver = 1 Gold. There is no standard fractional Copper.

Prices are intentionally contextual rather than globally fixed. Cost should reflect local supply, demand, danger, transport, quality, scarcity, law and bargaining position. Legal trade can include food, lodging, transport, tools, Gear, magical services, Skill Stones, Monster/Dungeon materials, healing, training, maps and information.

Wealth is uneven. A valuable reward should come from a giver who can plausibly afford it or from property/resources that actually exist. Do not inflate every adventuring job into treasure-scale economics.

blocks.b11:
The road dips toward Tidecross through a gap in the fields, and the walls grow with every step — grey stone, salt-stained near the base, tall enough that carts entering the gate look like beetles crawling under a doorframe. Traffic thickens: a fish cart, two women with bundles of washing, a boy leading a mule loaded with barrels. Nobody gives the blond stranger a second look beyond the usual glance at his sword.

Inside the gate the noise changes. Gulls. Rope creaking somewhere. A crier calling prices on haddock by the barrel. The main street runs downhill toward docks that smell of tar and brine, and side lanes branch off into warehouse shadows.

The Guild is not hard to find. A carved wooden sign hangs from an iron bracket two streets down on the left — crossed sword and arrow beneath a shield — and the building behind it is broad, timber-fronted, with tall windows and a steady stream of muddy boots going in and out. A pair of armed men lean against the wall by the door, chatting; one nods idly as the door swings.

Inside, warmth and noise. A long hearth burns on the left wall. The right side is a bar counter stacked with registers, and behind it a broad woman with iron-grey braids sorts papers. Boards along the back wall carry pinned notices, some vellum, some scrap. A dozen or so adventurers sit at trestle tables — a woman in oiled leather fletching arrows, two men arguing over a map, a young fellow asleep on his arms.

A clerk at the counter, a thin man with ink-stained fingers, looks up as Alaric approaches.

"Morning. Registering, or taking work? If it's work, I'll need to see a Guild plate first."

GUILD QUEST RANK CALIBRATION [GENERATION SCAFFOLD]

Guild Quest Rank is an institutional assessment of the responsibility, danger, uncertainty and expected capability of a contract:
NOVICE — routine local work, low institutional risk, ordinary early-career contracts.
PROVEN — established professional work with meaningful danger, uncertainty or responsibility.
VETERAN — serious professional assignments where reliable independent judgment is expected.
ELITE — high-risk or high-consequence contracts requiring exceptional competence.
MASTER — Half-Divine/B-rank-scale institutional work; rare and regionally significant.
GRANDMASTER — A-rank-scale strategic contracts; very rare and usually regional/international.
LEGEND — S-rank-scale strategic matters; exceptional, not ordinary local board filler.

Quest Rank belongs to the Guild's contract system. It does NOT alter the actual world to match the adventurer, and a listed Quest may prove easier, harder or differently complicated than expected because Guild information can be incomplete.

Do not use a public "Recommended Level" field in Guild presentation. The person's Power Rank and Guild Rank remain separate from Quest Rank.
GUILD CONTRACT BOARDS [CANON]
Every active branch keeps AT LEAST FIVE currently available contracts for each Guild Rank it supports. Small branches need not support every Rank; higher-rank work can arrive through regional or transnational Guild networks instead of five local Master or Legend crises.

The board changes once per in-world day, never as a full reroll: still-valid unresolved contracts stay; taken, completed, expired or withdrawn ones leave; new ones restore the minimum. Other adventurers take work, so an ignored contract can vanish, change or be resolved without Alaric. Listings Alaric has already seen stay the same until they change for such a reason.

Listings show the Quest Rank, never a Recommended Level. When Alaric reads a board, describe only the listings at his own Guild Rank (a glance at the rest at most) instead of reciting every Rank; most listings are routine standing work.
QUEST GENERATION — CAUSAL RULE [GENERATION SCAFFOLD]
A Quest is not content vending. It begins because someone or some institution wants the world to be different from how it is now.

Before generating a Quest, establish:
CAUSE — what current condition created the need?
STAKEHOLDER — who cares, and why?
KNOWLEDGE — how does the giver know there is a problem?
CAPABILITY GAP — why does the giver need outside help?
DESIRED STATE — what would count as success?
MEANS — what reward, authority, information or access can the giver realistically provide?

Generate Quests from existing people, places, shortages, threats, obligations, trade, politics, ecology, previous outcomes and newly established local conditions. Do not manufacture a crisis simply because Alaric is present.

GUILD BOARD MINIMUMS do not mean every new listing must be a fresh emergency. A branch can maintain its required pool through routine standing work, escorts, surveys, deliveries, material procurement, pest control, training support, investigation, repair/security work and regional-network contracts. The board should feel economically and institutionally plausible rather than like five catastrophes per Rank per day.
COMPLETE QUEST BODY [GENERATION SCAFFOLD]
When a new tracked Quest is actually offered, silently ensure it has:

1. TITLE — practical and locally meaningful.
2. GIVER — a real person/institution with authority or stake.
3. CAUSE — the existing problem/opportunity.
4. MOTIVE — why the giver cares.
5. DESIRED END STATE — what completion means.
6. QUEST RANK — for Guild contracts: Novice / Proven / Veteran / Elite / Master / Grandmaster / Legend. Private work has no Quest Rank unless the Guild lists it.
7. OBJECTIVE PATH — normally 1-4 meaningful steps; more only when fiction supports it.
8. ACCESS/KNOWLEDGE — what the player is told and what remains unknown.
9. COMPLETION EVIDENCE — how the giver can know the task is done.
10. REWARD SOURCE — why the reward exists and who can provide it.
11. CONSEQUENCE — what changes on success, failure, refusal or delay when relevant.

Do not pre-author every branch. Let branches emerge from player decisions and changing world state.

The <avereth> fact report still carries the Quest's hidden level (the Engine's Quest XP basis: the Level the task suits; for a Guild contract it lies inside its Quest Rank's band) and its type (minor/standard/dangerous/major scope). "Ink's on the table there." The clerk turns a heavy register sideways and slides it across the counter, along with a quill worn down to a stub. "Name — whatever name you mean to work under. Age. And a hand on the line confirming you've no standing feud with the Guild, the city, or the crown."

While Alaric writes, he pulls a blank copper plate from a drawer and stamps it with a small hammer blow, quick and practised. "Registration fee is two silver. Covers your plate, the first stamp, and access to the Novice board. You can leave the name field blank on the plate itself if you'd rather — plenty do — but the register keeps the true entry."

Down the hall, the two men at the map table raise their voices — "…no, the tide turns at midday, we'd be wading out…" — and the woman fletching arrows glances over once, then back to her work.

The clerk holds out a flat palm for the coin. "Two silver, and we're done. Quests post on the board by rank. Novice work only until your plate earns a stamp — rats, escorts, weed-cutting, that kind of thing. Questions, ask now, not after you've signed."

MATERIAL CULTURE / TRAVEL / COMMUNICATION [CANON]
Ordinary Avereth life is pre-industrial: handcraft, smithing, mills, farms, carts, horses, sailing vessels, fortified settlements, markets and written records. Mana and high magic can exceed mundane medieval capability, but they have not produced a default modern industrial society.

Ordinary long-distance communication uses letters, messengers, couriers and travelers. Magical long-distance communication can exist through powerful magic, institutions or artifacts, but is not universal on-demand infrastructure.

Ordinary travel is by foot, mount, wagon/carriage and ship. Distance consumes meaningful time. Teleportation or comparable transport may exist when explicitly established but is never assumed to be common public transit. Do not introduce firearms, engines, railways, electrical grids, telephones, computers or mass industrial production without explicit later canon.

The known world is dominated by one immense continent, Avereth, surrounded by ocean. Recorded history is extremely deep: civilizations, dynasties, religions and peoples have risen and vanished, and a few ancient beings remember eras ordinary people know only as legend.

The clerk takes the coins, marks the register, and stamps the copper plate with a second, cleaner blow. "Plate's your proof. Don't lose it — replacement's another silver. Board's on the back wall. Take a listing to the counter if you mean to take it, and we'll log it under your name."

The Novice board holds perhaps fifteen slips of paper and a few older notices gone brown at the edges. Five sit near enough to fresh to read plainly:

**RATS IN THE SALT CELLAR** — Novice. The Gull's Rest tavern, Harbor Lane. Cellar rats grown bold and big; keep out of the ale stocks. 8 silver on completion. See Keeper Dagny.

**GATE ESCORT: WOOL WAGON** — Novice. Farmer Hedwin Rool needs two blades to walk his wagon from the south gate to the market square, morning of next market day. Bandits unlikely, drunks likely. 5 silver each.

**WEED-CLEARING, FISH WEIRS** — Novice. Harbormaster's office. Kelp fouling the weir posts at the east shallows; cutting work, waist-deep, two days. 12 silver for the pair of hands. Bring your own knife.

**LOST DOG — REWARD** — Novice. Butcher's boy's dog, brown and white, last seen by the tannery ditches. 2 silver. May bite.

**STANDING: DOCK NIGHT WATCH** — Novice. Warehouse row, nights. Walk the row, report trouble, raise the watch bell. 4 silver a night, recurring. Guild logs attendance.

Behind, the clerk calls out to the room at large, "Anyone finished with the Gull's Rest slip? Dagny's asking." Nobody answers. The sleeping fellow doesn't move.

blocks.b23:
The clerk takes the slip, copies the title into a register, and stamps the corner. "Gull's Rest — down Harbor Lane, third building past the chandlery, you'll smell it before you see it. Quest's logged under Red. Report back to Dagny when it's done, and bring the slip or your plate." He hands the marked paper back and turns to the next customer.

Harbor Lane runs steep toward the water, cobbles slick with fish gut and morning dew. The chandlery announces itself with the reek of tallow and rope, and the third building past it is a squat timber tavern with a gull carved over the door, one wing chipped. Smoke curls from the chimney; a barrel of brine sits by the step.

Inside is dim and mostly empty at this hour. A woman with forearms like a smith's is hauling a crate onto the bar — Keeper Dagny, presumably, grey-streaked hair tied back with string. She sets the crate down and sizes up the newcomer, gaze dropping to the copper plate in his hand.

"Guild's sent someone already, then. About time." She jerks a thumb toward a low door behind the bar. "Cellar's through there. Rats have been at the grain sacks and one of the maids swears she saw one the size of her boot. You go down, you kill what's down there, and you don't crack my ale barrels doing it. Eight silver when the cellar's clean." She leans on the bar. "Anything bite you down there, that's your own affair. Still eight silver."

CLASS FRAMEWORK [CANON]
A Class is a major power path, not an absolute prohibition on learning outside Skills. The current standard Base Classes are:
Warrior — favored STR/VIT; direct martial offense with defensive depth.
Mage — favored INT/WIL; arcane offense, wards, mobility and control.
Guardian — favored VIT/WIL; protection, endurance and battlefield holding.
Duelist — favored STR/AGI; precision, mobility, tempo and counterplay.
Ranger — favored AGI/PER; ranged precision, positioning and hunting-oriented play.

Skills remain open-learn when a legitimate source exists. Class Affinity affects learning/proficiency speed rather than directly multiplying damage.

Later Class Evolutions are NOT a fixed prewritten tree. They emerge from actual development.

*Cool wind moves through the rough grass around Alaric Red's boots.*

*The last thing that belongs to Earth is still there in memory—an old life, a world without visible mana, Classes, or this impossible second beginning. The present is different: the smell of soil and distant woodsmoke, an unfamiliar sky, and stone walls beyond the public road.*

*Alaric Red is already standing on an uncultivated roadside verge outside the nearby city. Cultivated fields and fenced holdings begin farther away. No one is close enough to have witnessed the instant of arrival.*

*The body is Human, healthy, and eighteen years old. Simple traveler's clothes are already being worn; a small pouch holding five silver rests at the belt. The memories are still from Earth.*

*A translucent interface opens across Alaric Red's vision.*

`Origin: Earth`

blocks.b30:
LAW AND AUTHORITY [CANON + GENERATION SCAFFOLD]
Local rulers, civic authorities, courts, guards, militaries, landholders and customary institutions govern ordinary law. The Adventurers' Guild does not replace them.

When a legal issue matters, identify which authority actually has jurisdiction; what conduct is prohibited or owed; who can investigate, arrest, judge or collect; how status, evidence, Rank and local custom affect procedure; and what realistic limits constrain enforcement.

Law should create consequences and negotiation, not omniscient policing. Powerful individuals may be difficult to arrest, but Rank does not automatically erase property rights, contracts, local politics or social retaliation.
CURRENCY / EVERYDAY ECONOMY [CANON]
Common currency uses whole coins: 10 Copper = 1 Silver; 10 Silver = 1 Gold. There is no standard fractional Copper.

Prices are intentionally contextual rather than globally fixed. Cost should reflect local supply, demand, danger, transport, quality, scarcity, law and bargaining position. Legal trade can include food, lodging, transport, tools, Gear, magical services, Skill Stones, Monster/Dungeon materials, healing, training, maps and information.

Wealth is uneven. A valuable reward should come from a giver who can plausibly afford it or from property/resources that actually exist. Do not inflate every adventuring job into treasure-scale economics.
MATERIAL CULTURE / TRAVEL / COMMUNICATION [CANON]
Ordinary Avereth life is pre-industrial: handcraft, smithing, mills, farms, carts, horses, sailing vessels, fortified settlements, markets and written records. Mana and high magic can exceed mundane medieval capability, but they have not produced a default modern industrial society.

Ordinary long-distance communication uses letters, messengers, couriers and travelers. Magical long-distance communication can exist through powerful magic, institutions or artifacts, but is not universal on-demand infrastructure.

Ordinary travel is by foot, mount, wagon/carriage and ship. Distance consumes meaningful time. Teleportation or comparable transport may exist when explicitly established but is never assumed to be common public transit. Do not introduce firearms, engines, railways, electrical grids, telephones, computers or mass industrial production without explicit later canon.
GUILD CONTRACT BOARDS [CANON]
Every active branch keeps AT LEAST FIVE currently available contracts for each Guild Rank it supports. Small branches need not support every Rank; higher-rank work can arrive through regional or transnational Guild networks instead of five local Master or Legend crises.

The board changes once per in-world day, never as a full reroll: still-valid unresolved contracts stay; taken, completed, expired or withdrawn ones leave; new ones restore the minimum. Other adventurers take work, so an ignored contract can vanish, change or be resolved without Alaric. Listings Alaric has already seen stay the same until they change for such a reason.

Listings show the Quest Rank, never a Recommended Level. When Alaric reads a board, describe only the listings at his own Guild Rank (a glance at the rest at most) instead of reciting every Rank; most listings are routine standing work.
QUEST GENERATION — CAUSAL RULE [GENERATION SCAFFOLD]
A Quest is not content vending. It begins because someone or some institution wants the world to be different from how it is now.

Before generating a Quest, establish:
CAUSE — what current condition created the need?
STAKEHOLDER — who cares, and why?
KNOWLEDGE — how does the giver know there is a problem?
CAPABILITY GAP — why does the giver need outside help?
DESIRED STATE — what would count as success?
MEANS — what reward, authority, information or access can the giver realistically provide?

Generate Quests from existing people, places, shortages, threats, obligations, trade, politics, ecology, previous outcomes and newly established local conditions. Do not manufacture a crisis simply because Alaric is present.

GUILD BOARD MINIMUMS do not mean every new listing must be a fresh emergency. A branch can maintain its required pool through routine standing work, escorts, surveys, deliveries, material procurement, pest control, training support, investigation, repair/security work and regional-network contracts. The board should feel economically and institutionally plausible rather than like five catastrophes per Rank per day.
COMPLETE QUEST BODY [GENERATION SCAFFOLD]
When a new tracked Quest is actually offered, silently ensure it has:

1. TITLE — practical and locally meaningful.
2. GIVER — a real person/institution with authority or stake.
3. CAUSE — the existing problem/opportunity.
4. MOTIVE — why the giver cares.
5. DESIRED END STATE — what completion means.
6. QUEST RANK — for Guild contracts: Novice / Proven / Veteran / Elite / Master / Grandmaster / Legend. Private work has no Quest Rank unless the Guild lists it.
7. OBJECTIVE PATH — normally 1-4 meaningful steps; more only when fiction supports it.
8. ACCESS/KNOWLEDGE — what the player is told and what remains unknown.
9. COMPLETION EVIDENCE — how the giver can know the task is done.
10. REWARD SOURCE — why the reward exists and who can provide it.
11. CONSEQUENCE — what changes on success, failure, refusal or delay when relevant.

Do not pre-author every branch. Let branches emerge from player decisions and changing world state.

ENGINE NOTE:
The <avereth> fact report still carries the Quest's hidden level (the Engine's Quest XP basis: the Level the task suits; for a Guild contract it lies inside its Quest Rank's band) and its type (minor/standard/dangerous/major scope). Never show a Recommended Level in the story, on a board or in an NPC's words; the Guild speaks in Quest Ranks.
ALDERWATCH [CANON SEED]
A walled city in Valedorn Crown and a possible campaign starting city. Exact districts, economy, rulers and history are intentionally open.

GENERATION DIRECTION: let Alderwatch reflect central Valedorn — connected roads, layered civic/noble authority and access to the wider kingdom — while giving it one local economic purpose and one local pressure only when play needs them. Do not prefill the city with plot-critical institutions.
VALEDORN CROWN [CANON + REGIONAL SEED]
Position: central Avereth. Capital: Crownheart. Strongest human kingdom. Public S-ranks: 3.

Valedorn is a political center of human diplomacy with deep noble lineages, wealthy academies, old military institutions and one of the largest Adventurers' Guild headquarters. Its strength is breadth: population, wealth, administration, magic, military organization and diplomacy rather than one narrow specialty.

GENERATION FLAVOR: portray layered institutions, patronage, old rights, busy roads, provincial differences and court influence without making every scene court politics. Wealth and sophistication coexist with ordinary villages and practical local problems. Valedorn is powerful but coalitions can constrain it.

Blank space is intentional. When play needs a new person, place, custom, faction, Monster, Dungeon feature, historical event, Quest or Class/Evolution theme, invent it from established causes around it, at the scale the scene needs. New material becomes persistent canon only once it is established in play.
AVERETH — WORLD IDENTITY [CANON]
The known world is dominated by one immense continent, Avereth, surrounded by ocean. Recorded history is extremely deep: civilizations, dynasties, religions and peoples have risen and vanished, and a few ancient beings remember eras ordinary people know only as legend.

The tone is high fantasy with contrast. Safe cities, farms, workshops, trade, families, festivals and ordinary careers coexist with dangerous wilderness, Monsters, natural Dungeons, political violence and ancient powers. The world is not uniformly grim and is not built as a sequence of combat zones.

Current established great powers are six human kingdoms — Valedorn Crown, Caelreth, Veyrhold, Solmere, Ilyrion and Duskreach — plus two recognized monster realms, the Ashen Scale Dominion and Verdant Fang Court. Human and monster states are not unified species blocs; trade, diplomacy, rivalry, war and cooperation can cross species lines.

Material culture is Western-fantasy medieval alongside mana and high magic. Modern or industrial technology is not the default.

The road dipped toward Alderwatch's gate between hedged fields, and cart traffic thickened as it neared — turnips, firewood, a tanner's wagon that souring the air long before the wall did. Two guards in Crown colors worked the gate, waving through locals with a nod and taking a longer look at anyone with a weapon. One of them glanced at the sword at Alaric's hip, then at his face, and jerked his thumb toward the gatehouse stair.

"Adventurer, are you? Guild's registration's through the Guild, not here. Walk on. Don't draw it inside the walls."

Inside, the city opened into morning noise: cobbles slick from last night's washing, a bell somewhere, women arguing prices over baskets of eels. Alderwatch was busier than its walls had promised — three streets braided together at the gate square, signage in wood and painted iron. The Guild's crest, a crossed sword and arrow over a shield, hung from an iron bracket two streets up on the left, above a heavy door left open to the morning.

The hall inside smelled of lamp oil, leather and old ale. Long boards covered one wall with nailed-up notices, most stamped with red wax seals. A kill-board of sorts ran along another — horned skulls, a shed scale the size of a dinner plate, a claw. A dozen people milled about: a scarred woman restringing a bow in the corner, two men in mud-stiffened mail leaning at the rail by the quest boards, a robed figure reading at a table.

The front desk ran half the length of the room. Behind it sat a broad-shouldered man with a grey queue and a clerk's quill tucked behind one ear, tallying something in a register. He finished his line before he looked up.

"Morning. Registration, posting, or payout?"

The Adventurers' Guild is a neutral transnational institution for registration, certification, contracts, Monster/Dungeon information, rewards, material brokerage, frontier support and high-rank mediation. It does not replace rulers, courts, guards, militaries or property law.

POWER RANK and GUILD RANK are different systems.
Power Rank F / E / D / C / B / A / S is a person's objective Evolution state; it exists with or without Guild membership, and the Guild cannot grant it.
Guild Rank Novice / Proven / Veteran / Elite / Master / Grandmaster / Legend is institutional standing held only by registered members.
Standard correspondence: F -> Novice, E -> Proven, D -> Veteran, C -> Elite, B -> Master, A -> Grandmaster, S -> Legend. It is a promotion minimum, not identity: an E-rank member may still be Novice, and a non-member has no Guild Rank.

Guild contracts carry a Quest Rank with the same labels (the Guild's assessment of responsibility, danger and expected capability). Members normally take contracts of their own Guild Rank and below.

"Registration." The clerk set the quill down and pulled a fresh sheet from a stack, along with an inkwell whose lid was already cracked. "Right. Name?"

He dipped the quill and held it ready over the line, then looked up properly — a slow pass over the sword, the armor, the red eyes, cataloguing without comment.

"Here's how it goes. Five questions, your mark at the bottom, and one silver for the slate and the plate. That's the whole ceremony." He tapped the register. "New intake starts at Novice Rank. Novice takes contracts off the left half of that board there — escorts, pest work, deliveries, the like. Nothing on the right half until you've climbed, and the Guild checks the climbing itself, not me."

He smoothed the sheet flat with the side of his hand.

"Now. One — full name, spelled how you'd have me carve it. Two — age. Three — Class, if it's settled, and don't embellish; the plate reads what the assessor reads. Four — any Guild memberships elsewhere, Valedorn or foreign, yes or no. Five—" he nodded at the sword, "—armed work before, or is this your first? Answer honest. If you've never taken a contract, the Gate Assessors will know inside a week, and it goes worse for you then than it does being green now."

Behind Alaric, the two mailed men at the board rail drifted toward the desk's far end, one dropping a wax-sealed tag on the counter with a clack. The clerk held up a finger to them without turning his head.

"You're first in line. Go on."

LAW AND AUTHORITY [CANON + GENERATION SCAFFOLD]
Local rulers, civic authorities, courts, guards, militaries, landholders and customary institutions govern ordinary law. The Adventurers' Guild does not replace them.

When a legal issue matters, identify which authority actually has jurisdiction; what conduct is prohibited or owed; who can investigate, arrest, judge or collect; how status, evidence, Rank and local custom affect procedure; and what realistic limits constrain enforcement.

Law should create consequences and negotiation, not omniscient policing. Powerful individuals may be difficult to arrest, but Rank does not automatically erase property rights, contracts, local politics or social retaliation.
GUILD CONTRACT BOARDS [CANON]
Every active branch keeps AT LEAST FIVE currently available contracts for each Guild Rank it supports. Small branches need not support every Rank; higher-rank work can arrive through regional or transnational Guild networks instead of five local Master or Legend crises.

The board changes once per in-world day, never as a full reroll: still-valid unresolved contracts stay; taken, completed, expired or withdrawn ones leave; new ones restore the minimum. Other adventurers take work, so an ignored contract can vanish, change or be resolved without Alaric. Listings Alaric has already seen stay the same until they change for such a reason.

Listings show the Quest Rank, never a Recommended Level. When Alaric reads a board, describe only the listings at his own Guild Rank (a glance at the rest at most) instead of reciting every Rank; most listings are routine standing work.
QUEST GENERATION — CAUSAL RULE [GENERATION SCAFFOLD]
A Quest is not content vending. It begins because someone or some institution wants the world to be different from how it is now.

Before generating a Quest, establish:
CAUSE — what current condition created the need?
STAKEHOLDER — who cares, and why?
KNOWLEDGE — how does the giver know there is a problem?
CAPABILITY GAP — why does the giver need outside help?
DESIRED STATE — what would count as success?
MEANS — what reward, authority, information or access can the giver realistically provide?

Generate Quests from existing people, places, shortages, threats, obligations, trade, politics, ecology, previous outcomes and newly established local conditions. Do not manufacture a crisis simply because Alaric is present.

GUILD BOARD MINIMUMS do not mean every new listing must be a fresh emergency. A branch can maintain its required pool through routine standing work, escorts, surveys, deliveries, material procurement, pest control, training support, investigation, repair/security work and regional-network contracts. The board should feel economically and institutionally plausible rather than like five catastrophes per Rank per day.
COMPLETE QUEST BODY [GENERATION SCAFFOLD]
When a new tracked Quest is actually offered, silently ensure it has:

1. TITLE — practical and locally meaningful.
2. GIVER — a real person/institution with authority or stake.
3. CAUSE — the existing problem/opportunity.
4. MOTIVE — why the giver cares.
5. DESIRED END STATE — what completion means.
6. QUEST RANK — for Guild contracts: Novice / Proven / Veteran / Elite / Master / Grandmaster / Legend. Private work has no Quest Rank unless the Guild lists it.
7. OBJECTIVE PATH — normally 1-4 meaningful steps; more only when fiction supports it.
8. ACCESS/KNOWLEDGE — what the player is told and what remains unknown.
9. COMPLETION EVIDENCE — how the giver can know the task is done.
10. REWARD SOURCE — why the reward exists and who can provide it.
11. CONSEQUENCE — what changes on success, failure, refusal or delay when relevant.

Do not pre-author every branch. Let branches emerge from player decisions and changing world state.

The <avereth> fact report still carries the Quest's hidden level (the Engine's Quest XP basis: the Level the task suits; for a Guild contract it lies inside its Quest Rank's band) and its type (minor/standard/dangerous/major scope). Never show a Recommended Level in the story, on a board or in an NPC's words; the Guild speaks in Quest Ranks.
ALDERWATCH [CANON SEED]
A walled city in Valedorn Crown and a possible campaign starting city. Exact districts, economy, rulers and history are intentionally open.

GENERATION DIRECTION: let Alderwatch reflect central Valedorn — connected roads, layered civic/noble authority and access to the wider kingdom — while giving it one local economic purpose and one local pressure only when play needs them. Do not prefill the city with plot-critical institutions.
VALEDORN CROWN [CANON + REGIONAL SEED]
Position: central Avereth. Capital: Crownheart. Strongest human kingdom. Public S-ranks: 3.

Valedorn is a political center of human diplomacy with deep noble lineages, wealthy academies, old military institutions and one of the largest Adventurers' Guild headquarters. Its strength is breadth: population, wealth, administration, magic, military organization and diplomacy rather than one narrow specialty.

GENERATION FLAVOR: portray layered institutions, patronage, old rights, busy roads, provincial differences and court influence without making every scene court politics. Wealth and sophistication coexist with ordinary villages and practical local problems. Valedorn is powerful but coalitions can constrain it.
AVERETH — CANON AND GENERATIVE SPACE [AUTHORING RULE]
This lorebook is narrator/world knowledge, not knowledge any NPC automatically has. Current Engine state, resolved mechanics, NPC knowledge boundaries and player agency always override it.

Blank space is intentional. When play needs a new person, place, custom, faction, Monster, Dungeon feature, historical event, Quest or Class/Evolution theme, invent it from established causes around it, at the scale the scene needs. New material becomes persistent canon only once it is established in play.
AVERETH — WORLD IDENTITY [CANON]
The known world is dominated by one immense continent, Avereth, surrounded by ocean. Recorded history is extremely deep: civilizations, dynasties, religions and peoples have risen and vanished, and a few ancient beings remember eras ordinary people know only as legend.

The tone is high fantasy with contrast. Safe cities, farms, workshops, trade, families, festivals and ordinary careers coexist with dangerous wilderness, Monsters, natural Dungeons, political violence and ancient powers. The world is not uniformly grim and is not built as a sequence of combat zones.

Current established great powers are six human kingdoms — Valedorn Crown, Caelreth, Veyrhold, Solmere, Ilyrion and Duskreach — plus two recognized monster realms, the Ashen Scale Dominion and Verdant Fang Court. Human and monster states are not unified species blocs; trade, diplomacy, rivalry, war and cooperation can cross species lines.

Material culture is Western-fantasy medieval alongside mana and high magic. Modern or industrial technology is not the default.

"Alaric Red." The clerk wrote it out slow, quill scratching. "Eighteen. Warrior. No prior memberships. First armed work." Each answer got its own line; on the last he glanced up once more, and this time there was a flicker of something like approval. "Good. Honest's rarer than skilled."

He swept the silver off the counter into a drawer, then turned to a rack behind him and thumbed through stamped brass plates until he found a blank. He set it in a small press, wound a handle, and the room filled with a brief squeal of metal on metal. When he drew it out, the plate read ALARIC RED — WARRIOR — NOVICE, with the Guild's crest stamped above.

"Your plate. Don't lose it — replacement's another silver, and a plate found lying around is a plate someone else can use." He slid it across along with the register, spinning the book to face Alaric, quill offered handle-first. "Mark at the bottom. The line says you take contracts at your own risk, the Guild mediates disputes but doesn't avenge deaths, and rates are set by the posting party. Standard everywhere in Valedorn."

He waited for the mark, then blotted the page and closed the book.

"There. You're Novice, plate's live as of now." He tipped his chin toward the left half of the notice board. "Red wax seals mean the Guild's verified the poster. No seal, no contract — some fool posts a bounty on his neighbor's dog and expects us to enforce it. Contracts pay out here at this desk on return, and you bring proof — ears, tags, a receipt from the party you escorted."

Behind Alaric, one of the mailed men cleared his throat and rapped his knuckles on the counter.

"A moment, if you would. Fresh blood can read a board without me holding his hand."

The clerk's mouth twitched, but he turned to the men and picked up their wax-sealed tag, unrolling it against the wood.

The Novice board held the left half of the wall, and most of it was routine: standing notices for rat work in the granaries, a delivery run to a river village, grain-cart escort that repeated weekly. Paper had yellowed on some; a few carried fresh ink. The clerk's voice murmured behind at the counter, "—six hornwort, delivered whole, or it's half pay—" as Alaric read.

**GRANARY VERMIN CONTROL — Novice.** The Millwright's Row granary association wanted rats and whatever else was nesting under the floorboards cleared, three cellars, poison provided at cost. Pay: 8 silver. Proof: the cellarmaster's mark on the completion tag.

**ESCORT — CLOTH CART TO FERRY CROSSING — Novice.** Two days' road upriver, leaving tomorrow at dawn from the weavers' gate. A merchant's man would ride along. Pay: 12 silver each, up to four takers, meal at journey's end included.

**LOST DRAFT HORSE — Novice.** A carter's bay gelding had slipped its picket near the south pasture three days back, shod all four, a white blaze down the nose. Find it, bring it home or bring word where it fell. Pay: 5 silver.

**HERB PROCUREMENT — Novice.** An apothecary on Tanner's Lane wanted six bundles of hornwort gathered from the river shallows east of the walls, roots intact. Pay: 6 silver, baskets lent on deposit.

**WOLF SIGHTINGS, NORTH ROAD — Novice.** The caution slip was newer than the rest, red wax bright. Shepherds had lost two lambs near the north road mile-marker; tracks reported. The Guild wanted the sighting confirmed and the animals run off or killed if fewer than four. Pay: 15 silver, ears for proof. Someone had pinned a strip of paper beneath it in a different hand: *taken — J. Vess & partner, back by week's end.*

A young woman with ink-stained fingers came up beside the board, scanned past Alaric without a glance, and pulled the hornwort slip off its nail, tucking it into her sleeve before walking out.

blocks.b46:
The clerk was alone at the desk again — the mailed men had gone, their tag with them. He took the vermin slip, glanced at it, and pulled a smaller tag from a drawer.

"Granary work. Romantic, isn't it." He wrote Alaric's name on the tag, stamped it, and slid it over with the quest slip. "Take this to the cellarmaster at the Millwright's Row association — big granary with the sloped roof, can't miss it, follow the smell of grain. He marks it done, you bring it back here, eight silver. Poison's offered at cost if you want it, but that's between you and him." He was already looking past Alaric to the next arrival. "Next."

Millwright's Row sat south of the Guild hall, and the way there was all cart ruts and flour dust. Men hauled sacks up ramps; a boy swept spillage into a pail; somewhere a millstone droned through the wall. The association granary was the largest of the buildings, its foundation stones furred white at the joints, and a set of double doors stood open on the shade of the ground floor.

Inside, the air was cool and thick with grain and something else underneath — a sharp, sour note of nests and droppings. A barrel-chested man with sawdust in his eyebrows was nailing a board over a gap in the far wall, hammer swinging in slow, practiced strokes. He finished the nail before he turned.

"Guild?" He looked at the tag in Alaric's hand, then wiped his palms on his apron and came over. "Three cellars, all under this floor. Rats mostly, but there's something bigger working the west one — sacks torn open from below, that's no rat's teeth. Poison's in the green crocks if you want it. Or you've got a sword, I see." He jerked his thumb at a trapdoor by the stair. "Lantern's on the hook. Mind the third cellar ladder — bottom rung's cracked."

The trapdoor swung back on leather hinges, and a ladder led down into lamplight and shadow. The first cellar ran the length of the building overhead — low ceiling, floor packed earth, sacks stacked in rows with walkways between. Grain dust hung in the lantern's glow. It was warmer than the ground floor, close, and the sour nest-smell was stronger down here.

Signs of the work were everywhere. Droppings scattered along the base of the sack rows. Gnawed corners on the burlap, some sacks nibbled through at the bottom so a trickle of grain had fanned out onto the dirt like spilled sand. A wooden plank laid across two barrels — somebody's old attempt at a shelf — had been chewed along one edge.

Quiet, though. Whatever lived here had heard the trapdoor and gone still.

Alaric's boots crunched on spilled grain as he moved. Halfway down the cellar, along the wall furthest from the ladder, a heap of torn burlap sat shoved into the corner — pulled-down sacking, shredded fine, woven into something like a nest. A dark shape slipped between two sack rows as the lantern light swung toward it, low and quick, gone before it could be counted. Somewhere behind the stacked sacks came a faint, continuous sound: soft, busy scratching, many small feet, unhurried.

The walkways between the rows were narrow — shoulder-width, the sacks stacked chest-high on either side. From here, three ways led deeper: straight back toward the nest corner, left along the outer wall where the droppings thickened, or right, toward a darker stretch where the lamplight didn't reach and the sacks stood in taller stacks.

The scratching led him right, into the tall stacks where the lantern's circle shrank to a weak pool around his boots. The sound thickened as he went — not one place but many, a low rustle running along the tops of the sacks like wind through dry leaves, stopping when his light passed over it, starting again behind him.

Halfway along the row the droppings turned from scattered to heaped, a dark crust ground into the earth where the rats had worn their own path. Grain dust clung to it in greasy tufts of fur. The trail ran toward the outer wall, and there, at floor level, a gnawed hole the width of a fist opened into the foundation stones — the sour smell rolled out of it, thick enough to taste.

Rats worked that stretch openly. Two froze mid-step in the walkway ahead, blot-gray, each the length of a forearm with tail. A third sat on a torn sack at chest height, methodically dragging grain kernels into a gap between the burlap folds. None of them ran. They held still, black eyes fixed on the lantern, bodies tensed, and more shapes waited in the dark beyond the lantern's edge — the rustle of them never quite ceasing, all along the wall, close enough to hear breathing now.

The one on the sack shifted its grip on the kernel and bared its teeth, a small wet gleam, its weight rocking back onto its haunches.

CLASS FRAMEWORK [CANON]
A Class is a major power path, not an absolute prohibition on learning outside Skills. The current standard Base Classes are:
Warrior — favored STR/VIT; direct martial offense with defensive depth.
Mage — favored INT/WIL; arcane offense, wards, mobility and control.
Guardian — favored VIT/WIL; protection, endurance and battlefield holding.
Duelist — favored STR/AGI; precision, mobility, tempo and counterplay.
Ranger — favored AGI/PER; ranged precision, positioning and hunting-oriented play.

Skills remain open-learn when a legitimate source exists. Class Affinity affects learning/proficiency speed rather than directly multiplying damage.

Later Class Evolutions are NOT a fixed prewritten tree. They emerge from actual development.

A walled city in Veyrhold and a possible campaign starting city. Exact local details remain open.

GENERATION DIRECTION: make fortification, military traffic, hunting expertise or frontier logistics visible without turning the whole city into a barracks. Local economy and current border pressures should be established only when relevant.
VEYRHOLD [CANON + REGIONAL SEED]
Position: eastern Avereth. Capital: Ironward. Top-tier martial kingdom. Public S-ranks: 2.

Veyrhold is heavily militarized and shaped by dangerous borders. Martial training, disciplined officer corps, fortified cities and Monster-hunting traditions are central. Its most openly tense great-power relationship is with the Ashen Scale Dominion, though both avoid escalation into direct S-rank war.

GENERATION FLAVOR: fortification, logistics, readiness, veteran culture, border economies and social weight of service. Military presence should vary by location; civilians still trade, farm, marry, argue and live ordinary lives.
AVERETH — CANON AND GENERATIVE SPACE [AUTHORING RULE]
This lorebook is narrator/world knowledge, not knowledge any NPC automatically has. Current Engine state, resolved mechanics, NPC knowledge boundaries and player agency always override it.

Blank space is intentional. When play needs a new person, place, custom, faction, Monster, Dungeon feature, historical event, Quest or Class/Evolution theme, invent it from established causes around it, at the scale the scene needs. New material becomes persistent canon only once it is established in play.
AVERETH — WORLD IDENTITY [CANON]
The known world is dominated by one immense continent, Avereth, surrounded by ocean. Recorded history is extremely deep: civilizations, dynasties, religions and peoples have risen and vanished, and a few ancient beings remember eras ordinary people know only as legend.

The tone is high fantasy with contrast. Safe cities, farms, workshops, trade, families, festivals and ordinary careers coexist with dangerous wilderness, Monsters, natural Dungeons, political violence and ancient powers. The world is not uniformly grim and is not built as a sequence of combat zones.

Current established great powers are six human kingdoms — Valedorn Crown, Caelreth, Veyrhold, Solmere, Ilyrion and Duskreach — plus two recognized monster realms, the Ashen Scale Dominion and Verdant Fang Court. Human and monster states are not unified species blocs; trade, diplomacy, rivalry, war and cooperation can cross species lines.

Material culture is Western-fantasy medieval alongside mana and high magic. Modern or industrial technology is not the default.

LAW AND AUTHORITY [CANON + GENERATION SCAFFOLD]
Local rulers, civic authorities, courts, guards, militaries, landholders and customary institutions govern ordinary law. The Adventurers' Guild does not replace them.

When a legal issue matters, identify which authority actually has jurisdiction; what conduct is prohibited or owed; who can investigate, arrest, judge or collect; how status, evidence, Rank and local custom affect procedure; and what realistic limits constrain enforcement.

Law should create consequences and negotiation, not omniscient policing. Powerful individuals may be difficult to arrest, but Rank does not automatically erase property rights, contracts, local politics or social retaliation.
ADVENTURERS' GUILD — INSTITUTION AND RANK SYSTEMS [CANON]
The Adventurers' Guild is a neutral transnational institution for registration, certification, contracts, Monster/Dungeon information, rewards, material brokerage, frontier support and high-rank mediation. It does not replace rulers, courts, guards, militaries or property law.

POWER RANK and GUILD RANK are different systems.
Power Rank F / E / D / C / B / A / S is a person's objective Evolution state; it exists with or without Guild membership, and the Guild cannot grant it.
Guild Rank Novice / Proven / Veteran / Elite / Master / Grandmaster / Legend is institutional standing held only by registered members.
Standard correspondence: F -> Novice, E -> Proven, D -> Veteran, C -> Elite, B -> Master, A -> Grandmaster, S -> Legend. It is a promotion minimum, not identity: an E-rank member may still be Novice, and a non-member has no Guild Rank.

Guild contracts carry a Quest Rank with the same labels (the Guild's assessment of responsibility, danger and expected capability). Members normally take contracts of their own Guild Rank and below.

The road dips and rises with cart ruts dried hard as brick, and the walls of Redmarch grow as he walks—grey stone, high enough that the walkway on top shows the heads of two guards, the squat towers spaced along it dark-slit like arrow loops. Traffic thickens near the gate: a drover with six geese in a wicker crate, a woman leading a mule heaped with bundled fleeces, two boys arguing over a handcart with one cracked wheel. Woodsmoke and dung and something frying drift out on the wind.

At the gate a guard in Veyrhold's black-and-red checks the drover with a look and waves him through. When Alaric comes up, the guard's eyes go to the longsword at his hip, then to his face, and settle there a moment longer.

"Trading or looking for work?" the guard asks. Flat voice, bored, but the question has the rhythm of habit.

Whatever Alaric's answer, the man jerks his chin toward the gate. "In you go. Keep steel peace-bonded if you've got temper. Guild hall's up Coppergate, left side, the one with the antler over the door. Can't miss it."

Inside, the street noise changes—cloistered, echoey, loud with its own business. Stalls selling bread and bootlaces, a smith hammering somewhere out of sight, the smell of wet stone where runoff runs along a gutter. Coppergate climbs gently between timber-framed buildings leaning toward each other overhead.

The guild hall's antler is a full elk rack, iron-shod, mounted above double doors. Inside: a long hall smelling of tallow and old leather, benches scarred with knife-marks, a great board of pinned notices near the back, and a counter where a broad woman with a burn-scarred forearm is counting coins into a register while a lean man in a mud-caked hunting coat waits ahead of Alaric, arguing quietly about a bounty payout.

"—three days' work, Marta, and you're shorting me two silver on—"

"I'm shorting you nothing. The bounty said intact tusks. Yours came back chipped. Two silver or nothing, Corvan, and there's a queue behind you."

The man mutters, snatches coins off the counter, and shoulders past Alaric toward the door. The woman at the counter finishes her register line, looks up, and takes Alaric in—the sword, the armor, the face—with a practiced, unhurried eye.

"New face," she says. "Guild business?"

"Registration." Marta says the word like she's filing it before he's finished. "Right. Corner bench, second inkwell that actually has ink. Form's the short one—name, age, home settlement if you've got one, next of kin optional. Bring it back and I'll do the rest."

She turns to a shelf behind her, pulls a single sheet and a stiff board to lean it on, and sets both on the counter. "Read the back. It's the liability clause—Guild doesn't carry you out of a Dungeon, doesn't pay your funeral, doesn't avenge you. Some people sign without reading and then get loud about it later. Don't be one of them."

Behind him, the hall goes on with its own morning. Two women at the notice board pull down a pinned sheet and argue over the reward split. A boy sweeps sand across the flagstones near the door, unhurried. Somewhere past the counter a door swings and the smell of stew comes through—a kitchen somewhere in the back.

Marta leans a forearm on the counter, the burn-scar side. "One silver for the registration. That covers your Guild badge, the notice board, and the mediation rules—means if another member robs you, you come to us instead of finding a knife. After that, you take what contracts you like. Novice work only, at your level, and there's no shame in it. Everyone in this hall started there, whatever they claim now."

She glances at the sword on his hip, then back to his face.

"So. Name for the register, and your silver whenever you're ready."

blocks.b68:
Marta takes the form, holds it at arm's length, and reads it the way she counted coins—thoroughly, without hurry. "Alaric Red. Eighteen. No settlement, no kin." She dips a pen and copies the entries into a thick register with a worn leather spine, the page already crowded with other names in a dozen hands.

"One silver."

The coin crosses the counter. She bites it out of habit, drops it into the register drawer, and reaches under the counter for something else: a small badge of dull pewter, a stamped antler on its face, cold and lighter than it looks.

"Novice badge. Wear it or keep it on you—other members will want to see it before they trust you at their backs, and some contracts pay out only against the badge." She slides it across. "Badge number goes in the register with your name. If you're found dead, someone reads it off you and we know who to write to. You wrote nobody, so we'd write nobody. Worth thinking about someday."

She closes the register. "The board's that way, back wall. Novice work is on the low rows—anything without a colored ribbon is open to your rank. Red ribbon means Proven and up; don't pull those, the clerks get sour about it. Contracts pay on return, same counter as today. Anything with a Dungeon in it, you read twice and ask questions before you sign out."

The two women at the board have gone, leaving the pinned notices to flutter faintly in the draft from the door. The stew smell has thickened; someone behind the counter door calls out an order in a bored shout.

"That's you registered." Marta is already looking past him at the next arrival, a farm-handed boy hovering by the door with a dead fox over his shoulder. "Board's back there. Next!"

Local rulers, civic authorities, courts, guards, militaries, landholders and customary institutions govern ordinary law. The Adventurers' Guild does not replace them.

When a legal issue matters, identify which authority actually has jurisdiction; what conduct is prohibited or owed; who can investigate, arrest, judge or collect; how status, evidence, Rank and local custom affect procedure; and what realistic limits constrain enforcement.

Law should create consequences and negotiation, not omniscient policing. Powerful individuals may be difficult to arrest, but Rank does not automatically erase property rights, contracts, local politics or social retaliation.
NATURAL DUNGEONS [CANON]
Natural Dungeons are persistent supernatural ecosystems/resource zones shaped by concentrated mana and other established local conditions. They can contain unusual environments, rare materials, Skill Stones and exceptional Monsters.

A Dungeon is a physical world location, not a temporary game instance that appears for Alaric. It can be known, owned, disputed, exploited, sealed, partially mapped or ecologically connected to the surrounding region.

Exact layouts, ownership and local history remain open until established.
MONSTER ECOLOGY / FAUNA [CANON]
Native non-sapient fauna are part of Avereth's Monster ecology. Familiar animal-shaped creatures such as wolves, deer, horses, boars, bears and birds are mechanically Monsters with Level and Rank even when peaceful, domesticated or ecologically ordinary. 'Animal' remains normal everyday language for ecology/body type; it is not a separate rules category.

Monster classification does NOT mean hostility. Monsters are natural populations: they reproduce, compete, migrate, form territories/social structures, are hunted or domesticated, and may evolve through Ranks. Most ordinary fauna near settlements are F-rank; evolved higher-rank specimens become progressively rarer and more dangerous.

Sapience is separate from Monster classification. Some Monsters speak, organize societies, rule territory and conduct diplomacy.
GUILD CONTRACT BOARDS [CANON]
Every active branch keeps AT LEAST FIVE currently available contracts for each Guild Rank it supports. Small branches need not support every Rank; higher-rank work can arrive through regional or transnational Guild networks instead of five local Master or Legend crises.

The board changes once per in-world day, never as a full reroll: still-valid unresolved contracts stay; taken, completed, expired or withdrawn ones leave; new ones restore the minimum. Other adventurers take work, so an ignored contract can vanish, change or be resolved without Alaric. Listings Alaric has already seen stay the same until they change for such a reason.

Listings show the Quest Rank, never a Recommended Level. When Alaric reads a board, describe only the listings at his own Guild Rank (a glance at the rest at most) instead of reciting every Rank; most listings are routine standing work.

blocks.b72:
The notice board is a wall of overlapping paper, layered like feathers—new sheets nailed over old, corners curling, some so sun-bleached the ink has gone to ghosts. The low rows, unribboned, hold perhaps a dozen contracts. The handwriting varies with whoever posted them; the wax seals at the bottom of each vary too, some official, some just a thumbprint in candle drippings.

The nearest reads:

**BOAR DAMAGE — EASTFIELDS.** *Tusker rooting up barley plots near the mill. Tracks known. Farmer will add two silver from his own purse if the beast is brought down before the next full moon.* Guild bounty: 8 silver. Trophy: intact tusks.

Below it, in a clerk's neat hand:

**HERB GATHERING — GREYFEN.** *Fenroot and bitterleaf wanted, dried or fresh. Gathered from the fen edge only; the deep fen is posted off-limits by order of the Reeve.* Pays by weight, up to 6 silver.

A third, written in a lurching script with two blots:

**RATS — CELLAR OF THE BLUE OX TAVERN.** *Something's been at the grain cellar. Big, by the droppings. Get it out.* 4 silver and a hot meal. *(The "hot meal" is underlined twice.)*

Others further along: a lost goat, a caravan guard run to Ironward that wants two people, a notice about a Dungeon out past the mill roads—*Wormhole Delve, status: mapped, first three chambers open to Novice parties of three or more*—with a red ribbon tied at its corner anyway, and someone's charcoal scrawl beneath it: *asking for trouble, novices*.

A narrow man with ink-stained fingers and a clerk's cap is refilling the board's candle-lamp behind the notices, and he glances past the pinned sheets at the pewter badge in Alaric's hand.

"New blood," he says, without particular interest. "Take a sheet you mean to do, mind. Some of them pull the contract off the board when they sign it out. If you're only browsing, don't pull the nails."

Marta takes the rat sheet, checks the wax blot at the bottom against a register, and writes his badge number beside the listing. "Blue Ox. Down Copperlane, third turning past the well—follow the smell of frying fish and you'll see the sign. Ask for Bren the cellarman; it's his grain." She copies the contract, stamps it, and hands him his half of the paper. "Don't lose that. It's your proof of taking."

The walk is ten minutes through waking streets: a baker raking coals, two soldiers in Veyrhold grey laughing about something at a corner, a dog asleep in a doorway and uninterested in the world. The Blue Ox announces itself with a painted ox, blue-ish, over a wide door and a cellar hatch open in the cobbles beside it, breathing out a smell of damp stone and old grain.

Inside, the morning crowd is three carts' worth of drovers and a woman mending a net by the window. A heavy man behind the barrels—apron, forearms like hams—looks up.

"Guild?" He squints at the paper. "Rats, is it. Ha. Talk to Bren, down the hatch." He jerks a thumb. "Mind the third step. It's a liar."

The cellar stairs drop into cold dimness. Below, a stooped man with a lantern and a grain scoop is standing very still, staring at a heap of sacked barley against the far wall—where a corner of one sack has been torn open, and the spill beneath it is scattered in a way that suggests something dragged, not gnawed.

"Bout time," Bren says without turning. "It's not rats. Rats don't pull a sack off a stack."

blocks.b79:
Bren lifts the lantern higher without arguing, the light throwing long shadows down the ranks of sacks.

Alaric's boots crunch on spilled barley. The grain trail leads along the wall, past the stack, into the darker corner where the cellar meets the foundation stone—and there the wall is not wall. A gap yawns where the stones have buckled outward, earth showing through, a hole the width of a big dog's shoulders. Fresh dirt fans out from it across the floor.

The trail doesn't stop there. Something has scraped a shallow trough through the spill toward the cold corner behind the water cask, and as the lantern-light swings across it, Alaric catches the shape crouched there: low, bristled, grey-brown, built like a rat grown wrong—long of body, heavy in the shoulder, easily the size of a terrier, maybe bigger. Its eyes throw back two green coins. It is chewing on something, and it goes still the moment the light touches it, whiskers working, tail thick as a man's thumb lashing once against the stone.

Behind Alaric, Bren says, very quietly, "That'd be it, then," and starts backing toward the stairs without any hurry he doesn't absolutely need.

The creature's hindquarters coil. Its mouth opens on yellow teeth and a hiss like a kettle coming to the boil.
blocks.b80: *i lower my sword and dash forward with a Basic Attack at the creature*
blocks.b81:
Bren's lantern steadies in his fist as Alaric moves, boots loud on the stone, sword coming level.

The Gnawer doesn't wait to see how the charge ends. It springs sideways off the cold corner, a low skittering scramble, and puts the water cask between itself and the oncoming blade—tail lashing, teeth bared, a chittering hiss boiling out of its throat. Grain scatters under its claws. It is fast, faster than its bulk suggests, and it circles the cask's far side with its head low, tracking the sword's point.

Behind, at the stairs, Bren's voice comes down flat and quick: "Mind the wall—there's more than one hole down here. Where there's one of them—" He doesn't finish it. The lantern light trembles at the edge of vision, and the scratch of claws on stone has gone quiet, the creature holding still somewhere behind the cask.
blocks.b83:
The Gnawer explodes out from behind the cask before the sword can come around—low, fast, teeth first. It catches Alaric's shin through the boot leather, a sharp pinch and grind of yellow teeth, and then it is past him, scrambling for the breached wall.

But the blade is already swinging. The longsword comes down across its back mid-scramble, steel ringing on bone, and the Gnawer is driven flat into the grain spill with a crunch. It kicks twice, tail spasming against the stone, and goes still. A dark smear spreads slowly through the scattered barley.

The cellar is quiet again except for Bren's breathing at the top of the stairs. The lantern comes back down a step at a time.

"Dead, then." Bren leans over the rail to look, and lets out a long breath through his nose. "Where there's one of them there's a nest—mind you're not done yet, is all. That hole in the wall didn't dig itself." He comes the rest of the way down, scoop in hand like a weapon he forgot to put away, and crouches by the carcass, poking it once with the scoop's edge. "Terrier-sized. Marta'll want proof. Whole, if you can carry it."

blocks.b86:
MONSTER ECOLOGY / FAUNA [CANON]
Native non-sapient fauna are part of Avereth's Monster ecology. Familiar animal-shaped creatures such as wolves, deer, horses, boars, bears and birds are mechanically Monsters with Level and Rank even when peaceful, domesticated or ecologically ordinary. 'Animal' remains normal everyday language for ecology/body type; it is not a separate rules category.

Monster classification does NOT mean hostility. Monsters are natural populations: they reproduce, compete, migrate, form territories/social structures, are hunted or domesticated, and may evolve through Ranks. Most ordinary fauna near settlements are F-rank; evolved higher-rank specimens become progressively rarer and more dangerous.

Sapience is separate from Monster classification. Some Monsters speak, organize societies, rule territory and conduct diplomacy.
REDMARCH [CANON SEED]
A walled city in Veyrhold and a possible campaign starting city. Exact local details remain open.

GENERATION DIRECTION: make fortification, military traffic, hunting expertise or frontier logistics visible without turning the whole city into a barracks. Local economy and current border pressures should be established only when relevant.
VEYRHOLD [CANON + REGIONAL SEED]
Position: eastern Avereth. Capital: Ironward. Top-tier martial kingdom. Public S-ranks: 2.

Veyrhold is heavily militarized and shaped by dangerous borders. Martial training, disciplined officer corps, fortified cities and Monster-hunting traditions are central. Its most openly tense great-power relationship is with the Ashen Scale Dominion, though both avoid escalation into direct S-rank war.

GENERATION FLAVOR: fortification, logistics, readiness, veteran culture, border economies and social weight of service. Military presence should vary by location; civilians still trade, farm, marry, argue and live ordinary lives.
AVERETH — CANON AND GENERATIVE SPACE [AUTHORING RULE]
This lorebook is narrator/world knowledge, not knowledge any NPC automatically has. Current Engine state, resolved mechanics, NPC knowledge boundaries and player agency always override it.

Blank space is intentional. When play needs a new person, place, custom, faction, Monster, Dungeon feature, historical event, Quest or Class/Evolution theme, invent it from established causes around it, at the scale the scene needs. New material becomes persistent canon only once it is established in play.
AVERETH — WORLD IDENTITY [CANON]
The known world is dominated by one immense continent, Avereth, surrounded by ocean. Recorded history is extremely deep: civilizations, dynasties, religions and peoples have risen and vanished, and a few ancient beings remember eras ordinary people know only as legend.

The tone is high fantasy with contrast. Safe cities, farms, workshops, trade, families, festivals and ordinary careers coexist with dangerous wilderness, Monsters, natural Dungeons, political violence and ancient powers. The world is not uniformly grim and is not built as a sequence of combat zones.

Current established great powers are six human kingdoms — Valedorn Crown, Caelreth, Veyrhold, Solmere, Ilyrion and Duskreach — plus two recognized monster realms, the Ashen Scale Dominion and Verdant Fang Court. Human and monster states are not unified species blocs; trade, diplomacy, rivalry, war and cooperation can cross species lines.

Material culture is Western-fantasy medieval alongside mana and high magic. Modern or industrial technology is not the default.
blocks.b87:
Bren stays put at the foot of the stairs, scoop held two-handed, lantern raised. "Right you are," he mutters. "I'll mind the light."

The hole is tighter than it looked. Alaric turns sideways and eases through, stone rasping against his armor, sword leading. Beyond the breach the earth opens into a dug passage—claw-scored walls, a ceiling of packed dirt braced here and there by gnawed cellar joists the creature has dragged in. The smell is thick and animal: musk, urine, rotted grain. The air is cooler than the cellar and damp, and each breath stirs dust that tickles the throat.

Ten paces in, the passage forks. The left branch slopes down and goes dark past the reach of light spilling through the breach behind. The right branch is littered with plunder—shreds of burlap sack, a chicken bone, a child's-sized knuckle of wood that might once have been a toy, chewed on both ends—and along its wall, a mound of shredded cloth and dry grass matted flat in the shape of something that sleeps there.

From somewhere up the right-hand branch comes a sound: a soft, rhythmic nestling, then a second sound answering it. Small. Alive. More than one.

Behind him, faint through the hole, Bren's voice carries down the passage, hushed: "You living, stranger?"

The passage narrows going up the right-hand branch, ceiling low enough that the sword has to angle down. The plunder thickens underfoot: sackcloth, bone, a corroded belt buckle, all of it gnawed. The nest-mound resolves as he nears it—stripped sacking packed into a shallow bowl, and in the bowl, two pups. Pink-bellied, blind, no bigger than a man's fist, writhing against each other for warmth. The sounds he heard were them.

Beyond the nest the passage runs another few paces and ends at a second hole, wider than the first, bored upward at a slant. Faint daylight bleeds down it, grey through packed earth, and with the light comes a smell of old hay and something sweeter— spilled ale, maybe, from somewhere above. A way out to the yard, or the stable side.

The pups go silent at the vibration of boots, squirming blindly toward the sound of him.

Back at the fork, Bren's voice again, louder this time, strained: "Stranger. Anything? Say something, I can't hear nothing down there." A pause, then, muttering, more to himself: "Marta'll have my hide if the whole wall goes."

The passage holds still around him. No claws, no hissing—only the two blind creatures in the nest and the pale thread of daylight at the burrow's mouth.

GUILD CONTRACT BOARDS [CANON]
Every active branch keeps AT LEAST FIVE currently available contracts for each Guild Rank it supports. Small branches need not support every Rank; higher-rank work can arrive through regional or transnational Guild networks instead of five local Master or Legend crises.

The board changes once per in-world day, never as a full reroll: still-valid unresolved contracts stay; taken, completed, expired or withdrawn ones leave; new ones restore the minimum. Other adventurers take work, so an ignored contract can vanish, change or be resolved without Alaric. Listings Alaric has already seen stay the same until they change for such a reason.

Listings show the Quest Rank, never a Recommended Level. When Alaric reads a board, describe only the listings at his own Guild Rank (a glance at the rest at most) instead of reciting every Rank; most listings are routine standing work.
ADVENTURERS' GUILD — INSTITUTION AND RANK SYSTEMS [CANON]
The Adventurers' Guild is a neutral transnational institution for registration, certification, contracts, Monster/Dungeon information, rewards, material brokerage, frontier support and high-rank mediation. It does not replace rulers, courts, guards, militaries or property law.

POWER RANK and GUILD RANK are different systems.
Power Rank F / E / D / C / B / A / S is a person's objective Evolution state; it exists with or without Guild membership, and the Guild cannot grant it.
Guild Rank Novice / Proven / Veteran / Elite / Master / Grandmaster / Legend is institutional standing held only by registered members.
Standard correspondence: F -> Novice, E -> Proven, D -> Veteran, C -> Elite, B -> Master, A -> Grandmaster, S -> Legend. It is a promotion minimum, not identity: an E-rank member may still be Novice, and a non-member has no Guild Rank.

Guild contracts carry a Quest Rank with the same labels (the Guild's assessment of responsibility, danger and expected capability). Members normally take contracts of their own Guild Rank and below.
ALDERWATCH [CANON SEED]

blocks.b96:
*The road takes him through open fields, then between two stone gateposts where a rutted track joins the king's road. Cart wheels creak somewhere ahead. The walls of Alderwatch rise grey and mortared, higher than they looked from the verge, and the morning sun throws their shadow partway across the road.*

*The gate is busy but unhurried. A line of farmers' carts, a drover prodding geese along with a switch, two watchmen in dull mail leaning on spears by the arch. One of them looks Alaric over—the sword at his hip, the armor—and loses interest when nothing about him demands a second glance. Nobody asks his name or business. The archway swallows the light for a few strides, cold stone breathing around him, and then the city opens up.*

*Inside: cobbles worn smooth, the smell of bread and horse dung and woodsmoke all at once. A street of shops angles away from the gate, signage hanging on iron brackets—a farrier, an apothecary with bundles of dried herbs strung in its window, a chandler. Voices overlap in the local tongue, which his own understands without effort. A woman scolds a boy for dropping a basket of apples; apples roll and are chased.*

*The Guild hall is easy to find, a broad two-story building of timber and stone set back from the street, its doors standing open. A painted shield above the lintel shows a crossed sword and arrow.*

*Inside, the noise changes—boot heels on floorboards, low talk, the scrape of a whetstone. The hall runs deep: long tables with benches, a notice board thick with posted sheets, a wide counter along the right wall where three clerks work. A pair of hunters in oiled leather argue over a map at the nearest table. Behind the counter, a grey-haired man with a register open in front of him stamps a page and calls the next name without looking up—"Torv, your payout's ready"—while a young woman clerk at the far end of the counter taps through a stack of wooden Quest tags, sorting them.*

*The floor is his to cross. Nobody has marked him yet beyond a flick of a hunter's eyes at the sword.*
